content: Phossy jaw, also known as phosphorus necrosis of the jaw, is a severe and often fatal occupational disease that historically affected workers exposed to white phosphorus without adequate protective measures. This condition was most prevalent among individuals employed in the matchstick manufacturing industry during the 19th and early 20th centuries. Advances in industrial hygiene practices have since eradicated the conditions that led to this affliction. Chronic exposure to white phosphorus vapor, which was a key component in the production of matches from the 1840s to the 1910s, resulted in the deposition of phosphorus in the jawbones. This exposure not only caused significant damage to the jaw but also led to severe neurological complications, including brain damage. Workers suffering from this condition initially experienced excruciating toothaches and gum swelling. Over time, the jawbone would develop abscesses, a process that was both agonizing and disfiguring. The condition was further characterized by the emission of a foul odor due to the necrotic bone tissue, which made the affected individuals socially ostracized. As the disease progressed, the jawbones would gradually decay and, in some cases, emit a greenish-white phosphorescent glow in the dark. At this advanced stage, surgical removal of the affected jawbone was often the only intervention that could potentially save the patient’s life. Without such intervention, death from systemic organ failure was almost inevitable. Public outrage over the devastating effects of phossy jaw eventually led to significant changes in match manufacturing processes, effectively eliminating the disease. In some countries, legislative measures were necessary to compel the industry to adopt safer practices, as manufacturers were initially resistant to change. A related condition, osteonecrosis of the jaw, has been identified as a potential side effect of bisphosphonates. These are phosphorus-based medications widely used to inhibit bone resorption in the treatment of osteoporosis, bone metastases in cancer, and other bone-related conditions.
